digest.top_line: ASTRO brain mets guideline: SRS strong for ECOG 0-2 with up to 4 intact mets, conditional for 5-10; HA-WBRT plus memantine strong when WBRT used.
digest.tldr: Guideline and consensus day, no new efficacy readouts; CNS and oligo-mets carried it. ASTRO grades SRS strong for up to 4 brain mets, conditional for 5-10; ESTRO conditionally prefers 2x12Gy for painful vertebral mets. Common gap: dose/fractionation and re-RT rest on retrospective data or opinion, and the pelvic SABR re-RT Delphi split on cumulative OAR constraints.

sites.intro: ASTRO extends SRS to 5-10 intact mets on conditional, low-QoE grounds, anchored by JLGK0901.

studies.name: ASTRO Clinical Practice Guideline: Radiation Therapy for Brain Metastases
studies.tldr: SRS strongly recommended for ECOG 0-2 with up to 4 intact mets, conditional for 5-10; HA-WBRT plus memantine strong when WBRT is used.
details: 🔍 ASTRO task force guideline, 4 key questions; AHRQ systematic review, 97 studies, literature through Sept 2020

verdict.rationale: Guideline grading, not an outcome. Strong grades rest on RCTs in 1-4 mets; 5-10 mets, SRS dosing and systemic-therapy deferral rest on low-quality or observational evidence.
verdict.audience: Adults with intact or resected brain mets from nonhematologic solid tumors

studies.significance: The size-indexed dosing is the transferable piece: single-fraction 2000-2400 cGy under 2 cm, multifraction (2700 cGy/3 or 3000 cGy/5) at 3-4 cm, with BED10 ≥5000 cGy tied to better local control. After resection, cavity SRS carries nodular meningeal risk up to 28% at 1 yr, the reason preop SRS is being tested.
studies.monday_clinic: In ECOG 0-2 pts with 5-10 intact brain mets, this supports SRS alone as a conditional option over WBRT; it does not extend to 11-15 mets, where the supporting series held only 10 pts.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ASTRO task force guideline built on an **AHRQ systematic review** (97 studies, literature extended to Sept 2020). Recommendations graded by **strength and QoE**; consensus by modified Delphi with a **≥75%** agreement threshold (≥90% for expert opinion).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Radiotherapeutic management of **intact and resected brain mets from nonhematologic solid tumors**. Small cell lung cancer excluded from the KQ1 RCTs; CNS-active systemic therapy and surgery deferred to the ASCO/SNO/ASTRO guideline.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **<2 cm:** SF SRS 2000-2400 cGy (strong). **≥2 to <3 cm:** SF 1800 cGy or 2700 cGy/3 fx or 3000 cGy/5 fx (conditional). **≥3 to 4 cm:** multifraction preferred; SF up to 1500 cGy if chosen. SRS **>6 cm discouraged**. WBRT example 3000 cGy in 10 fx with **hippocampal avoidance** for favorable prognosis.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: SRS-alone grade rests on 5 RCTs in 1 to 3 (one up to 4) mets, with **N0574** showing worse neurocognition and QoL after SRS plus WBRT. The 5-10 extension leans on **JLGK0901**; dosing descends from **RTOG 90-05**. NCT01592968 (SRS vs WBRT, 5-15 mets) and **CCTG CE.7** (SRS vs HA-WBRT plus memantine) were unreported.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents ECOG 0-2 pts with up to 10 intact brain mets or a resected met, plus favorable-prognosis pts needing WBRT. Does not represent pts with 11-15 mets, SCLC, or hematologic primaries.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Literature closes Sept 2020, before the 5-15 mets phase III and CE.7 read out. Several Table 3 QoE grades and the KQ2 table are not cleanly attributable in the source extract.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The document draws its firmest line at **4 mets**, softens at 5-10, and stops at 10. Deferral of local therapy for CNS-active systemics is a **conditional MDT call**, and its failure mode (local progression in existing lesions) returns to the RT clinic.

studies.interpretation:
The guideline's weight sits on one well-populated question and several thin ones. SRS alone for up to 4 intact metastases in ECOG 0-2 pts earns a strong grade with high-quality evidence because 5 RCTs, N0574 among them, converged on the same trade: adding WBRT buys intracranial control, does not buy survival, and costs neurocognition. Everything outside that boundary is graded more cautiously, and the useful exercise for a reader is to notice exactly where the panel drew its lines and why.

The 5-10 extension rests on JLGK0901, a prospective observational registry, plus retrospective support, which is why it is conditional with low quality of evidence. The refusal to extend to 11-15 metastases is the most instructive call in the document. A large multi-institution series did include such pts, but only 10 of them, against 190 with 5-10 and 882 with 2-4. Reading an essentially empty subgroup as evidence of equivalence would have been easy; the panel declined. The guideline also predates the final report of the phase III SRS vs WBRT trial in 5-15 metastases (NCT01592968) and CCTG CE.7, which tests SRS against HA-WBRT plus memantine, a comparator the earlier SRS trials never faced. Either could move the 5-10 and 11-15 boundary, and the annual review cycle exists to absorb exactly that.

The dosing guidance is tidy but evidentially soft. No prospective comparative study has tested SRS dose or fractionation. The size thresholds descend from RTOG 90-05, a dose-escalation study in pts who had all received prior focal RT or WBRT, plus retrospective series showing poor control with 1500 to 1800 cGy single fraction for lesions of 2 cm or more. The BED10 ≥5000 cGy association comes from a retrospective multi-institution analysis. These are sensible anchors, but the 2-3 cm and 3-4 cm grades should be read as consensus built on retrospective data, not as demonstrated superiority of multifraction regimens.

The resected-cavity section carries a tension the recommendation does not resolve. Postoperative SRS is strongly recommended on randomized data, with surgical bed control of 72% vs 43% at 12 months against observation, yet the same move away from WBRT exposed nodular meningeal disease, reported as high as 28% at 1 year and associated with poor survival. Preoperative SRS is the obvious candidate fix, but its support so far is a retrospective comparison, which is why it sits as investigational rather than preferred.

The systemic-therapy recommendations are the weakest by the guideline's own account. There is no randomized comparison of upfront vs deferred local therapy with CNS-active agents, CNS response rates span roughly 30% to 75%, and up to 40% of pts progress early without any response. Upfront local therapy for symptomatic disease is graded strong; deferral in asymptomatic pts is a conditional judgment on lesion size, location, eloquence and access to surveillance. For an RT reader, the practical point is that the deferral decision is shared with medical oncology, but its predominant failure pattern, local progression in pre-existing lesions, lands back in the radiation clinic, often at a larger size where single-fraction SRS is no longer the preferred tool.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Size-indexed dosing is the transferable piece: SF 2000-2400 cGy under 2 cm, multifraction (2700 cGy/3 or 3000 cGy/5) at 3-4 cm, and BED10 ≥5000 cGy tied to better local control. SRS alone stays conditional at 5-10 mets and is not extended to 11-15.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Deferring local therapy for CNS-active systemic therapy is a conditional option only in asymptomatic pts; symptomatic mets get a strong recommendation for upfront local therapy. CNS response rates span roughly 30% to 75%, up to 40% progress early, and no randomized trial compares deferral with SRS.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Intact mets >4 cm carry a conditional recommendation for surgery, and neurosurgical discussion is suggested for any lesion causing mass effect regardless of size. After resection, cavity SRS is strongly recommended, but nodular meningeal disease up to 28% at 1 yr is driving study of preop SRS.

sites.intro: Two spine SBRT documents: ESTRO grades selection and dosing, and an international panel carries mobile-spine compartment CTV logic to the sacrum.

studies.name: International consensus on target volume delineation for sacral metastases and spinal SBRT
studies.tldr: Kappa 0.73 for GTV and 0.59 for CTV across 9 experts and 10 cases; consensus compartment-based sacral CTV built on a new eight-segment classification.
details: 🔍 Eight radiation oncologists + one neurosurgeon, 9 international centres, independently contoured 10 sacral SBRT cases
🔍 Panel: >7850 spine SBRT cases collectively, median 13 yr spine SBRT experience (range 7-18)
📐 Agreement scored with STAPLE; consensus contours generated at 80% confidence level
📊 Most CTV variability in Case 2 (kappa 0.41) and Case 4 (kappa 0.48), ala lesions encroaching VB/posterior elements
📊 Modified STAPLE CTV accepted by consensus in 9 of 10 cases; Case 5 predominant only, 6/9 (67%)

Entire GTV compartment plus adjacent marrow compartment at risk

details: 🔗 Extends compartmental logic of mobile-spine SBRT consensus (Cox et al., Redmond et al.), which excluded the sacrum
🔗 Cited sacral SBRT series: cumulative LC 86.5% at 1 yr, 78.7% at 2 yr
⚠️ No sacrum-specific pattern-of-failure data underpin the CTV
⚠️ Three experts preferred isotropic 0-5 mm margin over nerve root, bowel, insufficiency fracture concerns
⚠️ Bone-confined disease only; not epidural/paraspinal extension, re-irradiation, or postop

verdict.rationale: Expert contouring consensus, 9 experts on 10 cases; agreement is opinion against opinion, not outcome. No sacrum-specific pattern-of-failure data underpin it; external validation pending.
verdict.audience: Bone-confined sacral metastases, de novo SBRT (not re-RT or postop)

studies.significance: Compartmental, not margin-based: entire GTV compartment plus the adjacent marrow compartment at risk, with the ala ossification line usable to cap the CTV only when the GTV spares the ala, and any S1 ala involvement starting the CTV above the S1 VB. Thecal sac contoured to inferior S5 stands in for the cauda equina.
studies.monday_clinic: In bone-confined sacral metastases planned for de novo SBRT, this supports an SCS compartment-based CTV over an isotropic margin; it does not extend to epidural or paraspinal extension, re-irradiation, or the postoperative sacrum.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: International expert contouring exercise: **8 radiation oncologists + 1 neurosurgeon**, 9 centres, >7850 spine SBRT cases collectively, median 13 yr experience. Independent GTV/CTV contours on CT fused with T1, T2 and T1 post-gadolinium MRI; agreement by STAPLE at 80% confidence, kappa-scored.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **10 previously treated sacral metastasis cases**, selected for a range of size and location across S1 to S5, including ala, foraminal and epidural extension. Only experts at academic centres with a dedicated spine SBRT programme took part.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: CTV covers the **entire compartment holding the GTV plus the adjacent marrow compartment at risk**, mapped to SCS segments, with superior/inferior extent set by vertebral levels; **any S1 ala involvement** starts the CTV at the superior S1 ala. The ala ossification line may cap the CTV only when the GTV spares the ala. **Thecal sac to inferior S5** as cauda equina surrogate; lumbosacral plexus nerve roots per Yi et al.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Modified STAPLE CTV reached **consensus in 9 of 10 cases**; Case 5 predominant only at 6/9 (67%). RO STAPLE and NS CTV volumes did not differ.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Carries the compartmental CTV of the mobile-spine SBRT consensus guidelines (Cox et al. intact, Redmond et al. postoperative) into the sacrum, which those guidelines left out. ISRS guidelines support spine SBRT for specific indications but give no sacrum-specific contouring.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents bone-confined sacral metastases treated with de novo SBRT. Does not represent epidural or paraspinal extension, re-irradiation, or the postoperative sacrum.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Ten cases chosen to be representative, not consecutive, and the panel is academic-only. Experts endorsed a hand-modified average of their own contours, so **9/10 consensus is partly self-confirming**.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The lasting value is a shared classification that makes sacral pattern-of-failure analysis possible; it does not show compartment CTVs beat limited margins for local control. The cited sacral series' **78.7% LC at 2 yr** is the benchmark SCS-coded failure data would need to move.

studies.interpretation:
This is the sacral sequel to the mobile-spine SBRT contouring consensus work (Cox et al. for intact disease, Redmond et al. postoperatively), and its main contribution is a vocabulary rather than a validated target. The eight-segment sacral classification gives centres a shared way to describe where disease sits and what was covered, which is a precondition for any pattern-of-failure analysis. The CTV rules themselves transplant the compartment logic from the mobile spine, and that transplant deserves scrutiny. In the mobile spine the disc space plausibly limits craniocaudal spread, which is part of why a vertebral-level boundary feels natural. The sacrum has only fibrocartilage remnants, and the authors concede the contiguous bone may lack that protection. Yet the recommended superior and inferior extent is still set by vertebral levels, with the S1 ala as the only stated exception. Whether that is adequate is exactly what nobody yet knows.

The agreement figures should be read for what they measure. A GTV kappa of 0.73 and CTV kappa of 0.59 show that nine experienced academic contourers converge on ten selected cases; they say nothing about whether the converged contour is the right one. The acceptance step compounds this, because experts were asked to endorse a hand-edited average of their own contours, so consensus in 9 of 10 cases is partly self-confirming. The more informative signal is where agreement broke down. Cases 2 and 4 (kappa 0.41 and 0.48) were ala lesions encroaching on the vertebral body and posterior elements. That is the anatomy where a compartment CTV grows largest, and where three experts preferred an isotropic 0-5 mm margin, citing nerve root, bowel and insufficiency fracture risk. The guideline is least settled exactly where it changes the plan most.

The outcome context is thin. The one sacrum-specific imaging series the authors cite reported cumulative local control of 86.5% at 1 year and 78.7% at 2 years, with failure most often in the vertebral body together with paraspinal tissue, then isolated epidural progression. If that pattern holds, a bone-confined compartment CTV addresses the first failure mode only in part and the epidural mode not at all, and the recommendations explicitly exclude epidural and paraspinal extension. The population this document governs is therefore the subset least likely to fail in the ways already described.

For a radiation oncologist the practical value is standardisation for trials and multi-institution audit, not a demonstrated gain in control. Adopting it for bone-confined de novo disease is reasonable because the alternative is no shared rule at all; the toxicity cost of larger ala-inclusive volumes is the open trade. Two findings would show it wrong: a failure series with marginal recurrences clustered across vertebral levels (the CTV is too short craniocaudally), or one showing no excess failures with limited margins (the CTV is larger than it needs to be). The classification system is what makes either analysis possible, and that is the part of this paper most likely to last.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Compartmental, not margin-based: entire GTV compartment plus adjacent marrow compartment, ala ossification line usable as a cap only when the GTV spares the ala, and S1 ala involvement starting the CTV above the S1 VB. Thecal sac to inferior S5 sets the cauda equina surrogate.

open_questions: Does compartment-based sacral CTV improve local control vs limited margins?
Sacral plexus and nerve root dose tolerance with SBRT
Insufficiency fracture risk with larger ala-inclusive CTVs

studies.name: ESTRO Clinical Practice Guideline: SBRT for Spine Metastases
studies.tldr: 22 recommendations, 5 statements (≥75% consensus): SBRT above 1x18Gy equivalent (BED10=50Gy10), 2x12Gy conditionally preferred for painful vertebral metastases; mostly moderate/expert-opinion evidence.

verdict.rationale: Clinical practice guideline: 22 recommendations, 5 statements at ≥75% panel agreement. Authors state most rest on moderate or expert-opinion evidence, few randomized trials underneath.
verdict.audience: Vertebral metastases from solid malignancies; excludes re-RT and symptomatic MSCC

studies.significance: The guideline splits single fraction by dose: 1x16 or 1x18Gy is not recommended over 1x8Gy for pain, while single fraction >20Gy carries a VCF penalty fractionated SBRT avoids. That leaves 2x12Gy as the conditionally preferred palliative schedule, with the floor for durable LC set above 1x18Gy equivalent (BED10=50Gy10).
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with painful vertebral metastases from a solid primary, Bilsky 0-1, not frankly unstable, up to 3 contiguous segments and prolonged life expectancy, this supports considering SBRT over conventional RT; it does not extend to short life expectancy, symptomatic MSCC, or re-irradiation.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ESTRO clinical practice guideline built on a **PRISMA systematic review** (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane; Jan 2005 to Sep 2021, RTOG 0631 added April 2023). Grading followed the **ASTRO methodology**; consensus required **≥75% agreement**, yielding **22 recommendations and 5 statements** across four key questions.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Vertebral metastases from **solid malignancies**, painful or oligometastatic. SBRT selection gate: **not frankly unstable (SINS greater than 12 excluded), Bilsky 0-1, up to 3 contiguous segments, prolonged life expectancy**. Re-irradiation and symptomatic MSCC are out of scope.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Prescription **above 1x18Gy equivalent (BED10=50Gy10)**; de novo schedules 1x20Gy, 1x24Gy, 2x12Gy, 3x10Gy, 5x7Gy. **2x12Gy conditionally preferred** for palliation; 1x16 or 1x18Gy **not recommended** over 1x8Gy when pain/QoL is the goal. PTV margin **≤3mm (minimum 1mm)**, MRI-fused sim CT ≤1.5mm, intensity-modulated delivery, cord dose prioritized over target coverage.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: VCF is the dominant event at **6-14%**, rising with single fraction **>20-24Gy**; fractionated SBRT shows **no VCF excess vs CRT** (high-level statement). Myelopathy **0.4%** in >1,000 pooled de novo pts; pain flare **43% vs 33%** vs CRT, but routine steroid prophylaxis is **not recommended** (conditional).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The pain recommendations reconcile **CCTG SC.24** (24Gy/2fx beat 20Gy/5fx on complete response, 35% vs 14%) with **RTOG 0631** (16 or 18Gy/1fx lost to 8Gy, 41.3% vs 60.5%) by reading both as schedule-specific. ROBOMET and the Sprave phase II sit in support but were abstract-only or underpowered.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents de novo vertebral metastases from solid malignancies, painful or oligometastatic, meeting SINS/Bilsky/extent selection. Does not represent re-irradiation, symptomatic metastatic spinal cord compression, or short-life-expectancy pts needing only short-term pain control.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **LC benefit** rests on a single-center SC.24 sub-cohort (137 pts), and the narrative's 80-95% LC range does not match the recommendation's 80-90%. The search closed Sep 2021 with one trial added later, and **no medical oncologist voted** on the concurrent IO/targeted-therapy recommendation.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The practical output is a fractionation hierarchy: 2-5 fractions for most, single fraction >20Gy only where fracture management is available. **High-grade epidural disease** (separation surgery, cord-constraint dose escalation) stays unresolved and outside the evidence base.

studies.interpretation:
The guideline's most useful move is refusing to treat single-fraction spine SBRT as one intervention. RTOG 0631 and CCTG SC.24 are routinely cited against each other: the first found worse pain response with 16 or 18Gy in one fraction than with 8Gy, the second more complete responses with 24Gy in 2 fractions than with 20Gy in 5. The panel reads both as dose-and-schedule results rather than a verdict on the technique, recommending against 16 or 18Gy as a substitute for 8Gy when pain is the goal and conditionally preferring 2x12Gy. That reconciliation is defensible, but the two trials also differ in endpoint (overall pain response vs complete response), in the conventional comparator, and in epidural disease mandates, with RTOG 0631 requiring a 3mm cord gap and SC.24 excluding only symptomatic compression. Attributing the divergence purely to dose is an interpretive choice, not something either trial tested.

On local control, the evidence is thinner than the confident dose floor suggests. The threshold above 1x18Gy equivalent rests on a dose-response pattern across largely retrospective series and one randomized comparison of 24Gy single fraction against 27Gy in 3 fractions in oligometastatic pts, only 56% of whom had spinal lesions. The SC.24 local failure advantage, 14.8% vs 35.6% at 2 years, comes from a single-center sub-cohort of 137 randomized pts, not the full trial. That supports practice but should not be read as settled, and the guideline itself quotes its LC expectation as 80-95% in the narrative and 80-90% in the recommendation.

The tension the panel names honestly is fracture. Very high single-fraction doses buy LC at a VCF cost, and fractionated SBRT carries a high-level statement of no VCF excess over conventional RT. Read together, the dose and toxicity sections push most pts toward 2 to 5 fractions, with single fraction above 20Gy reserved for centers prepared to manage fractures. That is the decision a radiation oncologist actually changes on Monday.

Transferability is narrower than the title implies. The selection gate (not frankly unstable, Bilsky 0-1, up to 3 contiguous segments, prolonged life expectancy) mirrors trial eligibility, so the pain and LC benefits apply cleanly only there. High-grade epidural disease, the setting where a less invasive alternative to separation surgery would matter most, sits outside the evidence; only 2% of SC.24 SBRT pts had Bilsky 2 or 3. The technical recommendations are framed as reproducing the conditions under which trial outcomes were achieved, not as tested against alternatives, which is reasonable but means a center departing from them is extrapolating.

What would move this read: replication of 2-fraction SBRT outcomes outside high-volume centers, and prospective toxicity data for SBRT with concurrent immunotherapy or targeted agents, an area the panel flags as uncertain without a medical oncologist among its voting members.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Single fraction is split by dose: 1x16 or 1x18Gy is not recommended over 1x8Gy for pain, and single fraction >20Gy carries a VCF penalty fractionated SBRT avoids. 2x12Gy becomes the conditionally preferred palliative schedule, with PTV margin ≤3mm and cord dose prioritized over coverage.

open_questions: Optimal management of high-grade epidural disease (Bilsky 2-3)
Spine SBRT toxicity with concurrent immunotherapy or targeted therapy
Single-fraction >20Gy LC gain vs vertebral fracture cost

sites.intro: Pelvic SABR re-RT Delphi agreed on schedules and IMRT with daily verification, but not on interval (43%) or cumulative OAR limits.

studies.name: International Delphi consensus for pelvic SABR re-irradiation
studies.tldr: 66% of statements reached consensus among 23 international radiation oncologists; no agreement on a 12-month interval (43%) or cumulative OAR constraints.
details: 🔍 3-round international Delphi; 44 practice statements generated after Round 1
📊 Round 2: 29 statements reached consensus; 15 re-presented in Round 3

subdetails: 23 radiation oncologists in Round 1 (56% of 41 invited); 21 in Round 2, 22 in Round 3
Countries: Italy 6, USA 5, UK 4, Canada 2, Switzerland 2, France 1, South Korea 1
Sub-specialty: GU 19 (83%), lower GI 11 (48%), gyn 8 (35%)

studies.significance: The agreed schedules (30–37.5 Gy/5–6 fx or 21–27 Gy/3 fx, alternate days), IMRT and daily volumetric or fiducial verification are the technique layer you can borrow. Dosimetry stayed unresolved: cumulative OAR constraints, PTV Dmax ≤140% (73%) and a 12-month interval (43%). The recovery assumption in each plan is still an institutional call.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with a pelvic lesion overlapping prior pelvic RT dose, this supports SABR re-irradiation as an MDT-discussed alternative to exenteration, including with controllable extra-pelvic oligometastases; it does not extend to lesions directly invading a luminal OAR.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **3-round international Delphi**, Round 1 opened 27/10/2020 and Round 3 closed 22/03/2021. **44 practice statements** after Round 1; 29 reached consensus in Round 2 and 15 were re-presented in Round 3. Led by a UK organising group with pelvic SABR re-irradiation experience.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Panel of radiation/clinical oncologists who had published on pelvic SABR re-irradiation or were judged international experts by the organisers, **one per research group**. **23 of 41 invited (56%)** joined Round 1; 21 and 22 took part in Rounds 2 and 3.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Agreed schedules: **30–37.5 Gy in 5–6 fractions or 21–27 Gy in 3 fractions, alternate days**. Agreement also on IMRT or similar high-conformity planning, daily online volumetric or fiducial verification, MRI/PET-CT co-registration where it helps delineation, and TG-263 nomenclature. A PTV point maximum ≤140% **did not reach consensus (73%)**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **66% of statements reached consensus** overall. Consensus was not reached on the minimum interval between courses, maximum lesion number/size, or **cumulative OAR constraints**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Sits alongside the ESTRO ACROP Delphi on salvage SBRT for intraprostatic relapse, which the paper cites, but covers the whole pelvis. Its suggested optimal constraints apply **AAPM TG-101** de novo SABR limits cumulatively; less conservative options draw on the Abusaris, Smith and Paradis series.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with a pelvic target after prior pelvic RT where overlapping dose could push an OAR past tolerance, including those with controllable extra-pelvic oligometastatic disease. Does not represent lesions directly invading a luminal OAR, where the panel judged SABR re-irradiation not usually appropriate.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Organisers chose the experts and participants were offered authorship, which pulls toward a shared prior. A **GU-dominant panel (83%)** and a median caseload of 10/yr (range 10–100) leave gyn and rectal statements on a thinner base. The agreement threshold for consensus is not given in the source excerpt.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Agreement covers technique and selection boundaries carried over from de novo SABR. What stays open is the dosimetric core of re-irradiation: **how much recovery to assume, after what interval, and which cumulative constraint to honour**, which the authors name as research priorities.

studies.interpretation:
A Delphi panel measures where experts already agree, so its value lies less in the statements that passed than in the line it draws between technique, where practice has converged, and dosimetry, where it has not. Here the convergence is on the parts of pelvic SABR re-irradiation borrowed from de novo SABR: IMRT or similar high-conformity planning, daily online volumetric or fiducial verification, image co-registration for delineation, reproducible supine immobilisation, and alternate-day schedules of 30–37.5 Gy in 5–6 fractions or 21–27 Gy in 3 fractions. Few re-irradiation programmes would dispute any of that. Agreement on it mostly confirms that the panel shares a technical vocabulary.

The questions that decide whether a plan is safe did not reach consensus. The panel could not agree on a 12-month minimum interval from prior pelvic RT (43%), on caps for lesion number or size, on a 140% PTV point maximum (73%), or on cumulative OAR constraints. The comments on the interval are revealing: participants argued that previously delivered OAR doses and primary disease type mattered more than elapsed time. That position is coherent, but it moves the decision onto the cumulative constraint, which is exactly the other place the panel split. The reader gets a framework whose technical layer is settled and whose dose ceiling is not.

Read the constraint material with that in mind. The suggested optimal constraints apply AAPM TG-101 five-fraction de novo limits cumulatively. The less conservative options draw on the Abusaris, Smith and Paradis series plus illustrative AAPM recovery assumptions. Those are small retrospective experiences and a physics consult framework, not dose-response data for re-irradiated pelvic bowel or bladder. The table itself warns that the conservative approach may prevent delivery of a meaningful re-irradiation dose. Recovery allowances that differ by source make any single number look more certain than it is.

Two selection boundaries carry more weight than the rest. Direct invasion of a luminal OAR drew 90% agreement that SABR re-irradiation is not usually appropriate, while mere contact split the panel at 50%. A few participants offered a lower total dose, compromised PTV coverage, or close intra/inter-fraction monitoring as alternatives. That gap is where many real cases sit, and the paper offers no consensus for it. The statement with the largest clinical consequence positions SABR re-irradiation as an alternative to exenteration after MDT review. It rests on opinion, not comparative outcome data.

On methodology, the organisers built the panel from published or reputationally recognised experts, one per research group, and offered participants authorship. That design maximises expertise but also pulls toward a shared prior. The panel was weighted toward GU practice (83%), with fewer gynaecological and lower GI members, and median annual volume was 10 cases. Statements about rectal or gynaecological re-irradiation therefore stand on a thinner base than GU cases. The excerpt does not give the agreement threshold used to declare consensus, which matters when an item at 73% failed.

The authors' own reading is the right one: the agreed statements are a starting checklist, and the unresolved ones mark the research agenda. The panel also endorsed prospective recording of outcomes and toxicity. That is what would eventually turn the interval and constraint questions from opinion into data.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Agreed technique layer: 30–37.5 Gy/5–6 fx or 21–27 Gy/3 fx on alternate days, with IMRT and daily volumetric or fiducial verification. The dose ceiling is still open (cumulative OAR constraints, PTV Dmax ≤140% at 73%, 12-month interval at 43%), so recovery assumptions remain an institutional decision.

Validated cumulative OAR constraints with recovery assumptions

studies.name: GEC-ESTRO HNS critical review: skin superficial brachytherapy with flaps and customized moulds
studies.tldr: Thicker bolus permits >5 mm prescription depth: at 5 mm depth, 10 vs 5 mm bolus cuts surface Dmax 148% vs 187%; no dose-PROM data.
details: 📊 WG position: >5 mm prescription depth acceptable in selected large NMSC when interstitial BT or EBRT not viable
🔍 PRISMA review, PubMed to 31 May 2019, HDR Ir-192 superficial BT with flaps or moulds
⚠️ Evidence base is retrospective series, case reports and surveys; no clinical trial data

details.text: 📊 Bolus thickness at fixed 5 mm prescription depth, 6×6 cm CTV (TG-43 plan, Oncentra)

rows: Up to 20 mm (scalp SCC); 15 mm (cheek SCC); 9-10 mm in several series

details: 🔗 Jaberi (Co-60): at 10 mm depth, mould 5 → 20 mm cuts surface dose 250% → 150%
⚠️ Thicker bolus flattens gradient: dose spreads further beyond the CTV
⚠️ No published link between 125%-140% Dmax, 5 mm depth or 5 mm bolus and PROMs
📐 At 150% Dmax, EQD2 (a/b 3 Gy) spans 121.5 to 189 Gy across ACROP schedules (55% difference)

subdetails: All included studies used TG-43, which ignores missing scatter
MC deviation below 3% at 5 mm depth (Granero)
Up to 5% with Freiburg flaps from air between spheres (Vijande)
No reviewed paper defined how Dmax was calculated (bins, sample points)

verdict.rationale: Working-group position from retrospective series and surveys, no trials or dose-PROM data. Widens indications to >5 mm depth in selected cases; sets no new constraint.
verdict.audience: Large NMSC extending >5 mm deep, interstitial BT or EBRT not viable

studies.significance: At 5 mm depth on a 6×6 cm CTV, thickening bolus from 5 to 10 mm drops surface Dmax from 187% to 148% while widening R100-R50 from 16.0 to 18.7 mm. A percentage Dmax cap also ignores fractionation: at 150% Dmax, EQD2 (a/b 3 Gy) spans 121.5 to 189 Gy across ACROP schedules, so any skin constraint has to be read per schedule.
studies.monday_clinic: In a large NMSC infiltrating beyond 5 mm where interstitial BT or EBRT is not an option, this supports mould or flap BT with thicker bolus as acceptable practice rather than declining BT; it does not relax the 5 mm envelope for routine superficial lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: GEC-ESTRO H&N and Skin Working Group critical review, PRISMA search of PubMed to **31 May 2019**, English only. Included conference papers, surveys, case reports and reviews of NMSC superficial HDR Ir-192 BT. Paired with a TG-43 planning exercise on **6×6 and 10×10 cm** CTVs at depths of 3, 5, 10 and 20 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Guidelines cap prescription depth at **5 mm**; ABS and GEB cap surface Dmax at **125% for flaps, 140% for custom moulds**, with catheters ideally 5 mm from skin. ACROP schedules for moulds/flaps: 17–18 × 3 Gy, 10–12 × 4 Gy, 10–12 × 5 Gy, 8 × 5 Gy BID.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Clinical series have prescribed beyond 5 mm: up to **20 mm** (scalp SCC), 15 mm (cheek SCC), 10 mm (Kalaghchi, Lancellotta, Chan), 9 mm (Jumeau). In the ABS survey **2 of 16** centres treated to 7 and 8 mm; in a Canadian survey only **3/6** centres used a Dmax metric.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Sits against the GEC-ESTRO ACROP, ABS consensus, AAPM and GEB/SEOR-SEFM skin BT guidance, all built on expert practice. The Zaorsky meta-analysis (EBRT 9965 vs BT 553 pts) favored BT cosmesis but carried no bolus, gradient or prescription-point data, so it cannot validate any of these limits.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents large NMSC extending more than 5 mm from the skin surface, treated with HDR Ir-192 superficial BT via flaps or moulds when interstitial BT or EBRT are not viable. Does not represent routine lesions inside the 5 mm guideline envelope or interstitial skin BT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Deep-prescription series never report what fraction of pts were treated beyond 5 mm or their separate outcomes. Dmax is a single point, sensitive to DVH sampling settings, and the skin shows a volume effect, so a point constraint may not track toxicity at all.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Bolus thickness lets depth and surface hot spot be set independently, at the cost of a **shallower gradient** into deeper tissue, analogous to IMRT vs conformal. The WG declines to propose new Dmax or depth values and routes the question to the COBRA multicentre data project and a standardized reporting dataset.

studies.interpretation:
The useful contribution here is not the literature census, which the authors themselves describe as retrospective and thin, but the argument that prescription depth and surface hot spot are separable. The 5 mm depth ceiling shared by ACROP, ABS, AAPM and GEB guidance reads best as a proxy: with catheters resting on a standard 5 mm bolus, prescribing deeper drives surface dose up steeply, so the depth cap functions as a skin-dose cap by another name. The planning exercise makes the mechanism explicit. Once bolus thickness becomes a free variable, the inverse square law lets the 100% isodose reach deeper tissue while the surface maximum stays contained. The working group's acceptance of deeper prescriptions in selected large tumours follows from that physics, not from new outcome data.

The price is a flatter gradient, and the paper is candid about it. Moving the source away from skin spreads dose further past the CTV, the same bargain made going from conformal RT to IMRT. For a lesion over cartilage, bone or near the orbit, the widened R100-R50 is the parameter that should govern bolus choice, and the review explicitly warns against stacking bolus when it pushes dose into a nearby OAR. A planner building a nasal or periorbital mould should treat gradient and OAR dose, rather than surface Dmax, as the binding constraint once the bolus is thickened.

On confidence: every limit in current skin BT guidance rests on single-centre retrospective series, case reports and surveys, and the reviewers found no study relating Dmax, depth or bolus thickness to toxicity or cosmesis beyond dose per fraction and treated volume. That cuts in both directions. The existing limits are not shown to protect anyone, but relaxing them is not shown to be safe either; the series treating to 9, 10, 15 or 20 mm report good outcomes without isolating the deep-prescription subset. The endorsement is therefore a permission granted in the absence of harm signals, not a demonstrated equivalence.

Two methodological points deserve more weight than they receive in the conclusions. A percentage Dmax constraint ignores fractionation, and across the ACROP schedules the same 150% surface maximum maps to EQD2 between 121.5 and 189 Gy, so a single cap is not one biological constraint. And Dmax as reported depends on DVH sampling settings and on TG-43 assumptions that ignore missing scatter at the surface. Point Dmax may simply be the wrong quantity to constrain, and the authors' preference for a small-volume surface metric is the more defensible direction.

What would make the position wrong: if pooled registry data, with COBRA as the named vehicle, showed more late skin or deep-tissue morbidity in deep-prescription cases at matched surface Dmax, the extra low-gradient dose below the target would be the obvious suspect, and thicker bolus would have traded a visible hot spot for a hidden one. Until that data exists, the practical shift is narrow. For a large NMSC otherwise headed to EBRT or no local therapy, mould BT with thickened bolus becomes a defensible option, planned against gradient and adjacent organ dose rather than a fixed depth ceiling.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: At 5 mm depth on a 6×6 cm CTV, thickening bolus from 5 to 10 mm drops surface Dmax from 187% to 148% while widening R100-R50 from 16.0 to 18.7 mm. A percentage Dmax cap ignores fractionation: at 150% Dmax, EQD2 spans 121.5 to 189 Gy across ACROP schedules.
